title: Build a JWT-Authenticated Task API From Scratch — Full Node.js + SQLite Capstone Walkthrough
description:
This is the JavaScript Mastery Path capstone, built stage by stage: a Task Tracker API where users register, log in, and manage their own tasks through a JWT-protected REST API backed by SQLite. We go through the project layout and environment-driven config, the SQLite connection and schema, a clean repository layer for users and tasks, JWT signing and an auth middleware, register/login routes with bcrypt password hashing, a protected tasks resource with per-user ownership checks, a full Jest + supertest integration test suite running against an in-memory database, and finally a Dockerfile, docker-compose.yml, and a two-job GitHub Actions CI pipeline that lints, tests, and builds a Docker image on every push. Every line of code shown is pulled directly from the capstone lesson — nothing invented, nothing skipped.

Lessons covered in this video:
- https://sigilipelli.github.io/javascript-mastery-path/level-4/10-capstone-project/

beats.narration: By the time you reach the capstone of the JavaScript Mastery Path, you've covered closures, async patterns, architecture, and security. This project pulls it all together into one real service: a JWT-authenticated task tracker built with Node, Express, and SQLite, and we're building it stage by stage, the way you'd build it on the job.

display.heading: The Capstone: A Production-Shaped Task API

beats.narration: Let's start with the shape of the project. It's called task-tracker-api, and it splits cleanly into an auth module, a users module, and a tasks module, each with its own routes and repository, plus a db and config file that everything else depends on.

Notice the repository files — users.repository.js and tasks.repository.js. Those are the only files in the whole project that know any SQL. Everything else — routes, middleware, tests — talks to plain JavaScript objects and functions, so swapping SQLite for Postgres later only touches those two files.

display.code:
task-tracker-api/
  src/
    app.js                  # Express app wiring — routes, middleware, error handling
    server.js                # entry point — starts the HTTP server
    db.js                    # SQLite connection + schema setup
    config.js                # environment-driven configuration
    auth/
      auth.routes.js          # /auth/register, /auth/login
      auth.middleware.js      # JWT verification middleware
      tokens.js                # sign/verify JWT helpers
    users/
      users.repository.js
    tasks/
      tasks.routes.js
      tasks.repository.js
  tests/
    tasks.test.js             # Jest + supertest integration tests
  Dockerfile
  docker-compose.yml
  package.json
  .env.example
  .github/
    workflows/
      ci.yml

beats.narration: The dependencies tell the story: better-sqlite3 for the database, bcrypt for hashing passwords, jsonwebtoken for auth tokens, and Express for routing. On the dev side, Jest and supertest handle testing. The test script sets NODE_ENV to test and runs Jest with --runInBand, so tests execute one at a time against a shared database.

Every setting that changes between your laptop, CI, and production lives in one config object, pulled from environment variables with sane defaults — the port, the JWT secret, and the database path, which automatically switches to an in-memory SQLite database whenever NODE_ENV is test.
With config sorted, we've got everything routes and the database need without hardcoding a single value. Next: the actual database layer.
Now for storage. This project uses better-sqlite3 — a synchronous SQLite driver, so no async ceremony for a database call, and no separate database server to run locally.

db.js opens the database at whatever path config gives it, turns on write-ahead logging for better concurrency, then creates two tables if they don't already exist: users, with a unique email and a password hash, and tasks, where every row is tied to a user_id.

The users repository has exactly two operations: find a user by email, and create one. That's it — no ORM, just two prepared SQL statements wrapped in plain functions, which is exactly what a repository layer should be: a thin, testable boundary around your queries.
We can now store and look up users. But storing them isn't the same as knowing who's making a request — that's what tokens and middleware are for.

display.heading: Storage is done
display.subheading: Next: proving who's making the request

beats.narration: Authentication here has two halves: a small helper that signs and verifies JWTs, and a piece of Express middleware that every protected route can reuse.

signToken takes a user and signs a token containing their id and email, set to expire in one hour. verifyToken does the reverse, and — importantly — it just throws if the token's invalid or expired, so the caller decides what to do about that failure.

requireAuth pulls the token out of the Authorization header, expecting the standard 'Bearer' prefix. No token means an immediate 401. A present token gets verified; if that succeeds, the decoded payload is attached to req.user for every route downstream. If it fails, that's also a 401 — invalid or expired.
With signing and verification in place, we can finally build the routes that actually issue these tokens: registration and login.
Two POST routes, both doing real validation before they touch the database.

Register checks for an email, an eight-character-minimum password, and rejects duplicates with a 409 — before it ever hashes anything expensive. Only then does bcrypt hash the password with ten salt rounds, save the user through the repository, and sign a token back to the client.

Login mirrors that shape: look up the user by email, then compare the submitted password against the stored hash with bcrypt.compare. Only a match issues a token — everything else gets the same generic 401, so a wrong email and a wrong password look identical to an attacker.
Registration and login both return a working token. Now let's protect something with it — the actual tasks resource.
This is where the JWT actually pays off — every task belongs to a specific user, and the app has to enforce that on every single query.

The tasks repository always scopes by user_id. listForUser only returns that user's rows. findOwnedById looks up a task by id and user_id together — so even if someone guesses a valid task id that belongs to a different user, the query simply returns nothing.

tasksRouter.use(requireAuth) at the top means every route below it needs a valid token, no exceptions. The interesting line is in the PATCH route: it calls findOwnedById first, and returns a plain 404 if the task isn't found or isn't owned by this user — never confirming to a stranger that it exists at all.

app.js is just wiring: JSON body parsing, a health check, the auth routes mounted at /auth, the tasks routes mounted at /tasks, and a centralized error handler at the bottom that catches anything thrown or rejected upstream and turns it into a clean 500 instead of a stack trace leaking to the client.
Auth, users, and a protected tasks resource are all wired together. Now we need to prove it actually behaves correctly — that's what the test suite is for.
Because config.js switches to an in-memory SQLite database whenever NODE_ENV is test, this suite runs against a real, fresh database every time — zero mocking of the data layer.

display.heading: Stage 6: Testing with Jest & Supertest
display.subheading: Real HTTP requests, an in-memory database

beats.narration: The auth tests are straightforward: register a user and confirm a token comes back, register the same email twice and confirm the second attempt gets a 409, then confirm a wrong password on login gets a 401.

The tasks tests do the real work: confirm an unauthenticated request gets a 401, confirm a created task actually shows up when listing, confirm marking it done updates the response — and confirm that patching someone else's task returns a 404, proving the ownership check actually holds up under a real HTTP request.
Locally, it's npm install, copy the env example and set a real secret, then npm test — the whole suite runs in seconds against that in-memory database, no external services needed.

display.code:
npm install
cp .env.example .env    # then edit JWT_SECRET
npm test                 # runs the full Jest + supertest suite against an in-memory DB
npm run dev               # starts the API on http://localhost:3000

beats.narration: With a passing suite proving the ownership checks and auth flow work, the last piece is making this runnable anywhere — Docker and CI.
The last stage is making this something a team can actually run — not just something that works on your machine.

The Dockerfile is a single stage on node:20-slim: copy the package files, run npm ci with --omit=dev so dev dependencies like Jest never ship, copy the source, and set NODE_ENV to production before exposing port 3000.

display.code:
# Dockerfile
FROM node:20-slim AS base
WORKDIR /app

COPY package.json package-lock.json ./
RUN npm ci --omit=dev

COPY src ./src

ENV NODE_ENV=production
ENV PORT=3000
EXPOSE 3000

CMD ["node", "src/server.js"]

beats.narration: docker-compose.yml builds that image, maps port 3000, injects the JWT secret and database path as environment variables, and — this is the important part — persists the SQLite file on a named volume, so the database survives a container restart.

display.code:
# docker-compose.yml — runs the API with a persisted SQLite file on a volume
services:
  api:
    build: .
    ports:
      - "3000:3000"
    environment:
      JWT_SECRET: ${JWT_SECRET:-dev-secret-change-me}
      DB_PATH: /data/tasks.db
      PORT: 3000
    volumes:
      - task-data:/data

volumes:
  task-data:

beats.narration: One command, docker compose up --build, and the whole API is running with a persisted database, no manual setup on the host machine at all.

display.code:
docker compose up --build
# API available at http://localhost:3000, SQLite file persisted in the
# "task-data" named volume across container restarts

beats.narration: The GitHub Actions workflow has two jobs: lint-and-test installs dependencies, lints, and runs the Jest suite on every push and pull request; docker-build only runs after that job passes, and actually builds the Docker image, tagged with the commit SHA — so a broken image can never reach main.

display.code:
# .github/workflows/ci.yml
name: CI

on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
  pull_request:

jobs:
  lint-and-test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with:
          node-version: 20
          cache: npm
      - run: npm ci
      - run: npm run lint
      - run: npm test

  docker-build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    needs: lint-and-test
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: docker/setup-buildx-action@v3
      - run: docker build -t task-tracker-api:${{ github.sha }} .

beats.narration: If you want to keep going: swap SQLite for Postgres by touching only the repository layer, since routes and middleware never talk to SQL directly. Add rate limiting to login, structured logging, a health-ready check, and a Playwright end-to-end suite wired into this same CI pipeline.

display.heading: Where to go from here
display.subheading: Extend it into a real portfolio piece

beats.narration: This capstone brings together everything from the path — layered code you can test in isolation, authentication done properly, a CI pipeline that actually gates bad changes, and a container image anyone can run with one command. That's the real difference between a script and a service.

display.heading: You've completed the JavaScript Mastery Path
